analysis.one_liner: Bans unregulated 'soft money' spending that influences federal elections.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to committee on the day it was introduced, never received a vote, and died when the 106th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would amend the Federal Election Campaign Act to prohibit any person from spending money to influence a federal election unless that money is subject to the same contribution limits, bans, and disclosure rules that apply to ordinary campaign contributions. In plain terms, it would close the 'soft money' channel — the route by which corporations, unions, and wealthy donors gave large, largely unregulated sums to political parties for federal campaigns. The bill was referred to the House Administration Committee and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the 106th Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary voters and candidates without access to large donors would benefit, because campaign spending in federal races would have to flow through regulated, limited, and publicly disclosed channels instead of unlimited soft money. Candidates would spend less time raising unlimited sums from large donors, and voters would see more of who is paying for campaign activity.

how_it_helps.text: The bill prohibits spending any money to influence a federal election unless the funds are subject to the Federal Election Campaign Act's limitations, prohibitions, and reporting requirements [S2][S3].

That means money spent on federal campaigns would be capped, barred where contributions are barred, and publicly reported, closing the unregulated soft-money channel named in the bill's title and subject listing [S1][S3].

analysis.who_pays: The national political parties, which were the main collectors of soft money, and the corporations, unions, and wealthy donors who gave it would bear the cost: their unlimited, undisclosed channel for funding federal campaigns would be shut off.

drawbacks.text: The effective-date clause as written says the ban 'shall not apply with respect to elections occurring after January 1999,' which appears to exempt every future federal election and would leave the ban with little or no practical reach — a serious drafting flaw in the bill as introduced [S3].

Critics of soft-money bans generally argue that simply prohibiting one channel pushes money into harder-to-trace forms of political spending, such as issue advertising by outside groups, and that stricter limits and reporting burdens raise compliance costs for parties and campaigns — a cost an honest supporter would acknowledge.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The policy goal — ending unlimited soft money in federal elections — would directly benefit ordinary voters, and the main costs fall on parties and large donors rather than the public. But this particular bill was minimal: a single section with no enforcement machinery, and an effective-date clause that as written appears to exclude all elections after January 1999, potentially neutering the ban entirely. It reads more like a statement of principle than a workable statute.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Administration Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and it died when the 106th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Patsy Mink introduced the bill on January 19, 1999, the opening days of the 106th Congress [S5].
Three Democratic representatives cosponsored it, for a total of four sponsors, all Democrats [S4].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on House Administration on January 19, 1999 [S5].
The action history shows no further action — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor vote — before the Congress ended on January 3, 2001 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The national political parties and the large corporate, union, and individual donors who financed federal campaigns through unlimited soft money were better off, because the ban was never even considered and the channel stayed open for two more full election cycles.

sides.party_line_note: All four sponsors were Democrats — the sponsor plus three Democratic cosponsors — and the record shows no Republican support and no committee action on the bill [S4][S5].

industries.note: Soft money was the parties' largest unrestricted revenue stream for funding federal campaigns; the bill would ban spending unregulated money to influence federal elections [S2][S3]. Keeping soft money open served the parties' institutional interest against voters' interest in limited, disclosed funding.

Soft money let corporations, unions, and wealthy individuals give sums far above the limits on direct contributions; the bill would have required all federal-election spending to comply with those limits and bans [S2][S3]. Their financial interest in the bill ran against the public's interest in limiting big-money influence.
